I spent a year in Grand Forks, ND, with the Air Force. All in all, there is much good, and much bad, depending on how you look at things. Overall, I did enjoy my time there. First the bad:

Winter is serious in ND. We're talking snow and sub zero temperatures. It doesn't snow that terribly much, but ya get a foot or two and the winds seem to blow it from one end of the state back to the other - LOL. 40 below zero happens and it is always cold in the winter. So much so that believe it or not, you need to have an immersion heater fitted to the engine block of your car, and almost every major parking lot has electric outlet installed in the parking spaces so that you can plug in your car. Without it. it can become impossible to start an engine. This is not an exaggeration. You'll need a parka, and as much in the way of warm clothing, gloves, boots, etc, as possible. Summer is short ... and mosquitoes are thick around any water source, like swamps, lakes, or rivers. The State tree of ND is the telephone pole. The land is flat and the only trees are those planted as windbreaks and in parks more or less.

The good: The people are fantastic. Polite, friendly folk and in general, they'll make you feel at home. Good hunting for pheasants, fishing is big, especially ice fishing in the winter. The year I was there I actually got to see the Northern Lights which were really cool, but can't say if that's normal, just that I saw them often in the winter months I spent there. Very cool. The air's clean and outside the cities it's just open farmland more or less. Very small population ... but the cities have everything any city would have. You're not far from Minnesota, or Canada, where you'll find areas more like you're used to in Washington. Basically, like anywhere, it is what you make of it.

That's about what I can say after a year's experience. Get ready for serious winter ... but good folks and flat land. It's a harsh world, weather wise, but not that horrible, and I actually enjoyed my time there, even bundled up in forty below weather.
I was before the oil boom, though, which I'd forgotten about ... so many things may have changed. Who knows, the weather's the same for sure though.
Either way I really really do appreciate the advice.
